text: Every two years, Americans vote in an election where the president is not even on the ballot.
And yet, this single vote can decide whether the next two years bring new laws, or total gridlock.
Here is how the midterms really work, and what changes with, or without, a majority in Congress.
First, why are they called midterms?
A president serves a four-year term.
Halfway through, in November of the second year, voters choose a new Congress.
The date is fixed by law: the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
In two thousand twenty-six, that was November third.
That is why the president is not running, but the president's party very much is.
So what is Congress, exactly?
It is the branch of government that writes the laws and controls the money.
It has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
A new law must pass both of them, word for word, before it reaches the president.
Think of them as two locked doors. To get a law through, you need the key to both.
The House is the big room.
It has four hundred thirty-five voting members, and seats are shared out between the states by population.
California has dozens of representatives. Several small states have just one.
Every member serves only two years, so all four hundred thirty-five seats are up at every midterm.
To control the House, a party needs a majority: two hundred eighteen seats.
The Senate is the smaller room.
Every state gets exactly two senators, whatever its size. That makes one hundred.
Senators serve six years, and only about one third of the seats are up at each election.
So a party needs fifty-one seats for a clear majority.
But there is a twist. If the Senate splits fifty to fifty, the vice president casts the tie-breaking vote.
Here is a common misconception.
Many people think the midterms replace the whole Congress.
In reality, the entire House is up, but around two thirds of the senators keep their seats, whatever happens.
And it is not only Congress. Many states also elect governors, state lawmakers, judges and local officials on the same day.
Turnout is usually lower than in presidential years, which means every single vote weighs a little more.
To see why a majority matters, let's follow an imaginary law.
We will call it the Bridge Repair Act: a plan to fix old bridges across the country.
Step one: it must pass the House, by a simple majority.
Step two: it must pass the Senate.
Step three: the president signs it, and it becomes law. Or the president vetoes it, and it goes back to Congress.
But here's where it gets strange.
In the Senate, a simple majority is often not enough.
Under Senate rules, most bills can be blocked by a filibuster: senators can keep debate going so the bill never reaches a final vote.
In the Senate, most laws need not fifty-one votes, but sixty out of one hundred, to get past a filibuster.
There are some exceptions, especially for certain budget bills.
But for most laws, fifty-one is not the magic number. Sixty is.
Now, the scenarios.
Scenario one: unified government.
Imagine Party A holds the White House, the House and the Senate.
Our Bridge Repair Act can move quickly through both chambers, and the president is ready to sign.
The main obstacle is the sixty-vote rule in the Senate, unless Party A has a very large majority or wins over some members of Party B.
Supporters say this lets a government deliver on its promises. Critics say it leaves fewer checks on the party in power.
Scenario two: the House changes hands.
Now Party A keeps the White House and the Senate, but Party B wins the House.
The House decides which bills it votes on. If its leaders do not schedule the Bridge Repair Act, it simply stalls.
The House can also launch investigations into the administration, and it can vote to impeach officials.
To pass anything, both sides now have to negotiate. Some call that healthy compromise. Others call it gridlock.
Scenario three: the Senate changes hands.
Party A keeps the White House and the House, but Party B wins the Senate.
The Senate has a power the House does not: it confirms the president's choices for federal judges, cabinet members and ambassadors.
With the other party in control, those nominations can be slowed, changed or rejected.
Treaties also need two thirds of the Senate to be approved.
Scenario four: Party B wins both chambers.
Now Congress can pass its own version of the Bridge Repair Act, or a completely different plan, and send it to the president.
The president can veto it.
To override a veto, Congress needs two thirds in both chambers: about two hundred ninety votes in the House and sixty-seven in the Senate.
That is a very high bar. In practice, most vetoes stand, so each side holds a strong card, and deals become necessary.
Divided or not, there is one deadline nobody can avoid: the budget.
The federal fiscal year starts on October first.
If Congress and the president do not agree on funding in time, parts of the government can shut down.
Many federal workers are sent home, and services like national parks may close.
Shutdowns have lasted from a few hours to more than a month. And they can happen under any combination of majorities, because funding bills usually need sixty votes in the Senate too.
And there is a surprising pattern in history.
Since the Civil War, the president's party has lost seats in the House in almost every midterm election.
There are only a handful of exceptions, such as nineteen thirty-four, nineteen ninety-eight and two thousand two.
Political scientists offer several explanations: voters balancing power, or the other party's supporters being more motivated to turn out.
It is a pattern, not a law of nature. Each election is decided by voters, district by district.
So when does the change actually happen?
Not right away.
Under the Constitution, the new Congress begins on January third.
Until then, the outgoing members keep working, in what is called a lame duck session.
Then, in January, the new majorities take over, choose their leaders, and the next two years begin.
So, the midterms do not choose a president, but they decide how much a president can do.
Two chambers, two hundred eighteen and fifty-one, sixty votes for most laws, and two thirds to override a veto.
